pos: adj. (in battering rams, engines for breaking down a wall)
etymology: From batter, Old French batre, to beat. The Authorized Version uses it twice, both in Ezekiel, of the rams set against a city's gates in the enacted sign of Jerusalem's siege.
biblical_def: And lay siege against it, and build a fort against it, and cast a mount against it; set the camp also against it, and set battering rams against it round about. The command is given to Ezekiel personally, and it is one of the strangest assignments in the prophets. He is told to take a tile, pourtray upon it the city, even Jerusalem, and then conduct a miniature siege against the drawing: fort, mount, camp, battering rams, and an iron pan set for a wall of iron between himself and the city. Then he is to lie on his left side three hundred and ninety days and on his right forty, bearing the iniquity of the house of Israel and of Judah. A prophet became a diagram. The second use is in the great sword-of-Babylon oracle: at his right hand was the divination for Jerusalem, to appoint captains, to open the mouth in the slaughter, to appoint battering rams against the gates. The king of Babylon stands at the parting of the way casting lots, and the lot falls on Jerusalem — and Ezekiel means the reader to see God's hand governing the arrow. Paul takes the whole siege vocabulary and moves it: for the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): beating or striking against; a battering ram being an engine used by the ancients to beat down the walls of besieged places.
webster_full: BATTERING-RAM, n. In antiquity, a military engine used to beat down the walls of besieged places.
BATTER, v.t. To beat with successive blows; to beat with violence, so as to bruise or shake.
SIEGE, n. The setting of an army around or before a fortified place for the purpose of compelling it to surrender.
MOUNT, n. A bank or mound of earth raised against a besieged city.
STRONGHOLD, n. A fastness; a fort or fortress; a place of security.
scriptures: Eze 4:2
And lay siege against it, and build a fort against it, and cast a mount against it; set the camp also against it, and set battering rams against it round about.

At his right hand was the divination for Jerusalem, to appoint captains, to open the mouth in the slaughter, to lift up the voice with shouting, to appoint battering rams against the gates, to cast a mount, and to build a fort.
Eze 4:1
Thou also, son of man, take thee a tile, and lay it before thee, and pourtray upon it the city, even Jerusalem:
(For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds;)
corruption_summary: Spiritual warfare is either dismissed as superstition or reduced to a technique of rebuking and claiming; Paul locates it in the pulling down of arguments and the bringing of every thought captive to the obedience of Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: 2 Corinthians 10 is the passage most quoted about spiritual warfare and least often read to its end. Paul names the target in the next verse: casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ. The strong holds are arguments and pretensions, and the siege engines are truth, preaching, prayer, and obedience. That is far less dramatic than the technique-driven version and far more demanding, since it requires a man to do the work on his own thinking first.

Ezekiel's enacted siege guards a second point, which is the seriousness of the messenger's own cost. He drew the city, built the works against it, lay bound on his side for well over a year, ate bread by weight and drank water by measure, and lost his wife without mourning her, all as signs to a people who would not hear words. Ministry in Scripture is not delivered from a safe distance. The prophet carried the message in his body before the city carried the siege in its walls.
roots_summary: Hebrew kar (H3733), a battering ram; matsowr (H4692), a siege or entrenchment; dayeq (H1785), a siege-wall or fort.
roots_lines: Hebrew kar (H3733) — a ram, and so a battering ram; both occurrences are in Ezekiel.
Hebrew matsowr (H4692) — a siege, a mound, a besieging; lay siege against it.
Hebrew dayeq (H1785) — a bulwark or siege wall; build a fort against it.
Hebrew sollelah (H5550) — a mound cast up against a city; cast a mount against it.
Greek ochuroma (G3794) — a fortress, a strong hold; the pulling down of strong holds.

“to appoint battering rams against the gates” — the sword of Babylon oracle.
“the weapons of our warfare are not carnal” — where the vocabulary moves.

pos: n. (a long spear used by horsemen)
etymology: From Latin lancea, a light spear, through Old French. The Authorized Version uses it once, in the oracle against Babylon, of the weapons of the army God was bringing from the north.
biblical_def: They shall hold the bow and the lance: they are cruel, and will not shew mercy: their voice shall roar like the sea, and they shall ride upon horses, every one put in array, like a man to the battle, against thee, O daughter of Babylon. Jeremiah is describing the Medes, and he describes them without flattery: they are cruel, and will not shew mercy. Scripture is entirely willing to say that God uses wicked instruments to execute righteous judgments, and it never pretends the instruments are good. Isaiah calls Assyria the rod of mine anger and then announces judgment on Assyria for the pride with which it swung. Habakkuk could not understand how a holy God could use the Chaldeans, whose might is their god, and the answer he received was that the just shall live by his faith. Here the reason for Babylon's fall is stated plainly: I will render unto Babylon and to all the inhabitants of Chaldea all their evil that they have done in Zion in your sight, saith the LORD. And the last time the city falls, an angel cries it with a strong voice — Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a spear, an offensive weapon in form of a half pike, used by the ancients and thrown by the hand; in Scripture, the weapon of the horsemen brought against Babylon.
webster_full: LANCE, n. A spear; an offensive weapon in form of a half pike, used by the ancients.
SPEAR, n. A long pointed weapon, used in war and hunting, by thrusting or throwing.
ARRAY, n. Order; disposition in regular lines; hence, order of battle.
CRUEL, a. Disposed to give pain to others, in body or mind; inhuman; hard-hearted.
JUDGMENT, n. The sentence or doom pronounced on any person or thing.
scriptures: They shall hold the bow and the lance: they are cruel, and will not shew mercy: their voice shall roar like the sea, and they shall ride upon horses, every one put in array, like a man to the battle, against thee, O daughter of Babylon.
Behold, a people shall come from the north, and a great nation, and many kings shall be raised up from the coasts of the earth.
And I will render unto Babylon and to all the inhabitants of Chaldea all their evil that they have done in Zion in your sight, saith the LORD.
Rev 18:2

And he cried mightily with a strong voice, saying, Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen, and is become the habitation of devils, and the hold of every foul spirit, and a cage of every unclean and hateful bird.
corruption_summary: God's use of a wicked nation as an instrument is read as divine approval of that nation, or else as evidence that he is not sovereign over history; Scripture holds both, using Babylon and then judging Babylon for what it did.
corruption_paragraphs: The pattern is consistent across the prophets and it settles two questions at once. Assyria is the rod of God's anger, and Isaiah 10 then announces, I will punish the fruit of the stout heart of the king of Assyria, because he saith, By the strength of my hand I have done it. Babylon is God's hammer, and Jeremiah 51 renders to Babylon all their evil. The instrument is real, the sovereignty is real, and the instrument's guilt is real, because a wicked man acting freely and wickedly may nevertheless accomplish exactly what God ordained. Peter says the same of the greatest crime ever committed: him, being delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, ye have taken, and by wicked hands have crucified and slain.

This is why the dictionary will not read national success as divine endorsement in any age. Cruelty is named as cruelty here even while the armies do God's work — they are cruel, and will not shew mercy. And Habakkuk's question, how the Holy One could use such men, is answered not by softening the instrument but by lengthening the view: the vision is yet for an appointed time; though it tarry, wait for it. Babylon falls in the end, twice over, and the last fall is final.
roots_summary: Hebrew kiydown (H3591), a lance, javelin, or short spear; 'akzariy (H394), cruel; gemuwl (H1576), a recompense.
roots_lines: Hebrew kiydown (H3591) — a lance, a javelin, a target; they shall hold the bow and the lance.
Hebrew 'akzariy (H394) — cruel, fierce; they are cruel, and will not shew mercy.
Hebrew shalam (H7999) — to make whole, to recompense, to repay; I will render unto Babylon.
Hebrew ra'ah (H7451) — evil, wickedness, calamity; all their evil that they have done in Zion.
Hebrew bath (H1323) — a daughter; against thee, O daughter of Babylon.

“they are cruel, and will not shew mercy” — the instrument named honestly.
“I will render unto Babylon” — and then judged.

pos: n. (the rudder or steering gear of a ship)
etymology: Old English helma, a rudder or tiller. The Authorized Version uses it once, in James's argument about the tongue, of the very small helm that turns a great ship.
biblical_def: Behold also the ships, which though they be so great, and are driven of fierce winds, yet are they turned about with a very small helm, whithersoever the governor listeth. James is building an argument out of three small things that control large ones: a bit in a horse's mouth, a helm on a great ship, and a little fire that kindles a great matter. Then the application: even so the tongue is a little member, and boasteth great things. His conclusion is the least flattering assessment of human speech in the Bible — the tongue can no man tame; it is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison. Therewith bless we God, even the Father; and therewith curse we men, which are made after the similitude of God. Out of the same mouth proceedeth blessing and cursing. My brethren, these things ought not so to be. And the standard he sets at the head of the chapter is impossibly high and deliberately so: if any man offend not in word, the same is a perfect man, and able also to bridle the whole body. James is not offering a technique for better communication. He is showing a man his heart through his mouth.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the instrument by which a ship is steered, consisting of a rudder, a tiller, and in large vessels a wheel; in Scripture, James's figure for the tongue.
webster_full: HELM, n. The instrument by which a ship is steered, consisting of a rudder, a tiller, and in large vessels a wheel.
RUDDER, n. The instrument by which a ship is steered; that part of the helm which consists of a piece of timber.
GOVERNOR, n. He that governs; one who steers, directs or controls; a pilot.
BRIDLE, v.t. To restrain, guide or govern; to check, curb or control.
TONGUE, n. The instrument of taste and of speech; the power of articulate utterance.
scriptures: Jas 3:4
Behold also the ships, which though they be so great, and are driven of fierce winds, yet are they turned about with a very small helm, whithersoever the governor listeth.
Jas 3:5
Even so the tongue is a little member, and boasteth great things. Behold, how great a matter a little fire kindleth!
Jas 3:8
But the tongue can no man tame; it is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison.
Jas 3:2
For in many things we offend all. If any man offend not in word, the same is a perfect man, and able also to bridle the whole body.
corruption_summary: Speech is treated as self-expression that carries no moral weight, or reduced to a communication skill to be improved; James makes the tongue the index of the heart and says no man can tame it.
corruption_paragraphs: Two modern accounts of speech both fail at James 3. The first says that words are merely expressive and that sincerity settles their morality — I was only being honest. The second treats speech as a skill set to be trained, so that the cure for a cruel tongue is a course in communication. James says the tongue is a fire, a world of iniquity, set on fire of hell, and that no man can tame it. That is not a problem of technique. The Lord had already located the source: out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh, and by thy words thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned.

The particular sin James presses is the double mouth: therewith bless we God, even the Father; and therewith curse we men, which are made after the similitude of God. The argument turns on the image of God in the person being cursed, which means every contemptuous word about another human being is a word about someone God made in his own likeness. A fountain does not send forth at the same place sweet water and bitter. Since no man can tame the tongue, the cure is not self-mastery but a new heart, and then the slow bridling that follows it — and the wisdom from above, which is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, and easy to be intreated.

“If any man offend not in word, the same is a perfect man” — the standard set.

pos: n. (a low vessel driven by oars; the warship of the ancient Mediterranean)
etymology: From Greek galea through Old French galie. The Authorized Version uses it once, in Isaiah's vision of a Jerusalem whose broad rivers no enemy warship can enter.
biblical_def: But there the glorious LORD will be unto us a place of broad rivers and streams; wherein shall go no galley with oars, neither shall gallant ship pass thereby. The picture is precise. Great rivers made cities rich and also made them reachable: the Tigris carried Assyria's ships and the Euphrates carried Babylon's. Isaiah promises Jerusalem the benefit without the exposure — broad waters that no war galley can navigate, because the river is the LORD himself. The chapter is full of the same exchange, the terrible scattering of the enemy and then the sight that replaces it: thine eyes shall see the king in his beauty; they shall behold the land that is very far off. And the centre of the passage is the great triple confession: for the LORD is our judge, the LORD is our lawgiver, the LORD is our king; he will save us. Judge, lawgiver, king — the whole civil order gathered into one Person, which is exactly the settlement Revelation reaches when John is shewn a pure river of water of life, clear as crystal, proceeding out of the throne of God and of the Lamb.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a low flat-built vessel with one deck, navigated with sails and oars, used chiefly in the Mediterranean; in Scripture, the warship that cannot enter Zion's rivers.
webster_full: GALLEY, n. A low flat-built vessel with one deck, navigated with sails and oars.
OAR, n. An instrument for rowing boats, being a piece of timber round or square at one end, and flat at the other.
GALLANT, a. Gay; well dressed; showy; splendid; magnificent.
LAWGIVER, n. One who makes or enacts a law; a legislator.
SECURITY, n. Freedom from danger; safety; freedom from fear or apprehension.
scriptures: But there the glorious LORD will be unto us a place of broad rivers and streams; wherein shall go no galley with oars, neither shall gallant ship pass thereby.
For the LORD is our judge, the LORD is our lawgiver, the LORD is our king; he will save us.
Thine eyes shall see the king in his beauty: they shall behold the land that is very far off.
Rev 22:1
And he shewed me a pure river of water of life, clear as crystal, proceeding out of the throne of God and of the Lamb.
corruption_summary: Security is sought in defences a people can build, and the offices of judge, lawgiver, and king are distributed among men as if they were ultimate; Isaiah gathers all three into the LORD and makes him the city's river.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 33:22 is one of the great political verses of the Old Testament and it is not a manifesto for any human arrangement. The LORD is our judge, the LORD is our lawgiver, the LORD is our king. All three offices belong finally to One, which is why no human magistrate may claim any of them absolutely and why the dictionary holds that family, church, and state each hold delegated authority in their own sphere under Christ. A state that gathers all three to itself has claimed the verse for a creature.

The security promised is equally unlike anything a city could build. Not walls but water — broad rivers and streams that carry no enemy galley. Psalm 46 says it the same way: there is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God. Jerusalem had no river; that is the point. The safety of the people of God has never been a matter of defensible terrain, and the last picture Scripture gives of the city has a river in it flowing from the throne, with the nations healed by the leaves on its banks.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'oniy shayit (H590, H7885), a ship of oars; 'addiyr (H117), mighty or gallant; choqeq (H2710), a lawgiver.

“Thine eyes shall see the king in his beauty” — what replaces the fear.

pos: n. (the bow or forepart of a vessel)
etymology: From fore and ship, rendering Greek prora, the prow. The Authorized Version uses it once, in the shipwreck narrative, where the sailors pretended to cast anchors out of the foreship while planning to flee.
biblical_def: And as the shipmen were about to flee out of the ship, when they had let down the boat into the sea, under colour as though they would have cast anchors out of the foreship. Luke describes a piece of deception with a sailor's eye: putting out anchors from the bow was a plausible manoeuvre, and it gave the crew a reason to lower the boat they meant to escape in. Paul saw through it and said to the centurion and to the soldiers, Except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved. The soldiers cut the ropes and let the boat fall off. What makes this the theological centre of the chapter is the promise it sits beside. An angel had already told Paul, Fear not, Paul; thou must be brought before Caesar: and, lo, God hath given thee all them that sail with thee — a guarantee that not one of the two hundred and seventy-six would be lost. Paul repeats it in the morning: there shall not an hair fall from the head of any of you. And in the same breath he insists the sailors must stay aboard. The certainty of the end did not make the means optional; it established them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the forepart of a ship; the prow; in Scripture, where the shipmen pretended to cast anchors while planning to escape.
webster_full: FORESHIP, n. The fore part of a ship.
PROW, n. The forepart of a ship; the bow.
ANCHOR, n. An iron instrument for holding a ship at rest in water.
MEANS, n. That which is used to effect an object; the instrument or agency.
DECREE, n. In theology, a predetermined purpose of God.
scriptures: And as the shipmen were about to flee out of the ship, when they had let down the boat into the sea, under colour as though they would have cast anchors out of the foreship,
Paul said to the centurion and to the soldiers, Except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved.
Saying, Fear not, Paul; thou must be brought before Caesar: and, lo, God hath given thee all them that sail with thee.
Wherefore I pray you to take some meat: for this is for your health: for there shall not an hair fall from the head of any of you.
corruption_summary: God's decree is set against the necessity of means, so that an assured outcome is taken to make effort pointless; Acts 27 gives the absolute promise and the absolute requirement in the same night, on the same deck.
corruption_paragraphs: Fatalism reasons that if none shall be lost, it cannot matter whether the sailors stay. Paul reasons the opposite way and the narrative vindicates him: except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved. The Reformed doctrine of the decree has always included the means within the thing decreed. God ordains that a man shall be saved, and ordains the preaching he will hear; he ordains that a harvest shall come, and ordains the ploughing. The soldiers cut the ropes of the boat because the promise was true, not in spite of it.

The chapter also shows what assurance actually does to a man in a crisis, which is not passivity but usefulness. Paul takes bread, gives thanks to God in presence of them all, tells everyone to eat for their health, and is the steadiest person aboard a ship that has seen neither sun nor stars in many days. He had a word from God, he believed it, and the belief made him practical. Wherefore, sirs, be of good cheer: for I believe God, that it shall be even as it was told me.
roots_summary: Greek prora (G4408), the prow or foreship; agkura (G45), an anchor; sozo (G4982), to save.
roots_lines: Greek prora (G4408) — the prow, the forepart of a ship; the foreship of Acts 27:30.
Greek agkura (G45) — an anchor; as though they would have cast anchors.

Greek sozo (G4982) — to save, to bring safely through; ye cannot be saved.

“Except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved” — the means inside the promise.
“there shall not an hair fall from the head of any of you” — the promise itself.

etymology: From Old French havot, plunder; the old cry havock was the signal for a general pillage. The Authorized Version spells it with the -ck and uses it once, of Saul's campaign against the church.
biblical_def: As for Saul, he made havock of the church, entering into every house, and haling men and women committed them to prison. The verse follows the stoning of Stephen, at which Saul was consenting unto his death, and it is deliberately domestic: not a policy pursued at a distance but a man going house to house, dragging out men and women. The result recorded by Luke is one of the great ironies of the book. At that time there was a great persecution against the church which was at Jerusalem; and they were all scattered abroad throughout the regions of Judaea and Samaria — and then, therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word. The campaign designed to destroy the church distributed it. Philip went down to Samaria; the gospel reached the Ethiopian on the Gaza road; men of Cyprus and Cyrene preached to Greeks at Antioch, and a great number believed. And the man who made the havock wrote afterwards, with no attempt to soften the record: who was before a blasphemer, and a persecutor, and injurious: but I obtained mercy, because I did it ignorantly in unbelief.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): waste; devastation; wide and general destruction; in Scripture, Saul's house-to-house campaign against the church at Jerusalem.
webster_full: HAVOCK, n. Waste; devastation; wide and general destruction.
HALE, v.t. To pull or draw with force; to drag.
PERSECUTION, n. The infliction of pain, punishment or death upon others unjustly, for adhering to a religious creed.
SCATTER, v.t. To disperse; to dissipate; to separate or remove things to a distance from each other.
MERCY, n. That benevolence, mildness or tenderness of heart which disposes a person to overlook injuries.
scriptures: Act 8:3
As for Saul, he made havock of the church, entering into every house, and haling men and women committed them to prison.
Act 8:1

And Saul was consenting unto his death. And at that time there was a great persecution against the church which was at Jerusalem; and they were all scattered abroad throughout the regions of Judaea and Samaria, except the apostles.
Act 8:4
Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word.
Who was before a blasphemer, and a persecutor, and injurious: but I obtained mercy, because I did it ignorantly in unbelief.
corruption_summary: Persecution is treated as an interruption of God's work rather than an instrument of it, and the persecutor as beyond the reach of grace; Acts 8 records the scattering that spread the gospel, and the chief persecutor writing epistles a few chapters later.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke's narrative refuses to describe the persecution as a setback. The church had been commanded to be witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth, and it had settled comfortably in Jerusalem. Saul's havock is what moved it. That is not a sentimental reading of suffering: men and women were haled to prison, Stephen was dead, and Luke names the grief — devout men carried Stephen to his burial, and made great lamentation over him. Both things stand. The cost was real and the mission advanced through it.

The second refusal is the more personal one. Paul never allowed his past to be softened in the retelling; he called himself the chief of sinners and said he persecuted the church of God and wasted it. And he drew from that the doctrine that keeps the door open for everyone: howbeit for this cause I obtained mercy, that in me first Jesus Christ might shew forth all longsuffering, for a pattern to them which should hereafter believe on him to life everlasting. If Saul of Tarsus is a pattern, no one is beyond it.
roots_summary: Greek lumainomai (G3075), to ravage or make havock; suro (G4951), to drag or hale; diaspeiro (G1289), to scatter abroad.
roots_lines: Greek lumainomai (G3075) — to outrage, to ravage, to make havock; the one occurrence, Acts 8:3.
Greek suro (G4951) — to drag, to haul; haling men and women.
Greek diaspeiro (G1289) — to scatter abroad as seed; they were all scattered abroad.
Greek euaggelizo (G2097) — to announce good news; went every where preaching the word.
Greek eleeo (G1653) — to have mercy on; but I obtained mercy.

“they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word” — what it produced.
“a blasphemer, and a persecutor, and injurious: but I obtained mercy” — the man's own account.

pos: n. (a hostile entry into another's territory)
etymology: From Latin invadere, to go in upon. The Authorized Version uses it once, in the mouth of an Egyptian servant left for dead by the Amalekites, reporting the raid that had burned Ziklag.
biblical_def: We made an invasion upon the south of the Cherethites, and upon the coast which belongeth to Judah, and upon the south of Caleb; and we burned Ziklag with fire. The speaker is a sick Egyptian slave abandoned in a field, whom David's men fed with bread and figs and raisins before he would talk. David had come home to find Ziklag burned and every wife and child taken, and his own men speaking of stoning him. What the chapter is known for is the verse in the middle of that: David was greatly distressed; for the people spake of stoning him, because the soul of all the people was grieved, every man for his sons and for his daughters: but David encouraged himself in the LORD his God. Then he did the thing he always did at his best — David enquired at the LORD, saying, Shall I pursue after this troop? And the answer came with the outcome attached: Pursue: for thou shalt surely overtake them, and without fail recover all. And he did: David recovered all that the Amalekites had carried away. He also settled the law of the spoil that day, that as his part is that goeth down to the battle, so shall his part be that tarrieth by the stuff.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a hostile entrance into the possessions of another; particularly, the entrance of a hostile army into a country for the purpose of conquest.
webster_full: INVASION, n. A hostile entrance into the possessions of another; particularly, the entrance of a hostile army.
INROAD, n. The entrance of an enemy into a country with purposes of hostility; a sudden or desultory incursion.
SPOIL, n. That which is taken from others by violence; plunder; pillage; booty.
DISTRESS, n. Extreme pain; anguish of body or mind; affliction; calamity.
ENQUIRE, v.i. To ask a question; in Scripture, to seek direction of the LORD.
scriptures: We made an invasion upon the south of the Cherethites, and upon the coast which belongeth to Judah, and upon the south of Caleb; and we burned Ziklag with fire.

And David was greatly distressed; for the people spake of stoning him, because the soul of all the people was grieved, every man for his sons and for his daughters: but David encouraged himself in the LORD his God.
And David enquired at the LORD, saying, Shall I pursue after this troop? shall I overtake them? And he answered him, Pursue: for thou shalt surely overtake them, and without fail recover all.
And David recovered all that the Amalekites had carried away: and David rescued his two wives.
corruption_summary: Encouragement is sought in circumstances, in a leader's own resolve, or in the support of his people; David's men were about to stone him and he encouraged himself in the LORD his God, then asked God what to do.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Samuel 30:6 is one of the most useful verses in Scripture for a man in leadership on his worst day, and the order of its clauses is the whole lesson. David was greatly distressed — the distress is granted, not denied. The people spake of stoning him — his support was gone. The soul of all the people was grieved, every man for his sons and for his daughters — and their grief was legitimate, since David's own decisions had left Ziklag unguarded. There is no circumstance left to draw on and no innocence to appeal to. But David encouraged himself in the LORD his God, which is an act, not a feeling, and it is the only source left when everything else is burned.

What follows is the pattern the dictionary keeps. He did not act on the encouragement by charging out; he enquired at the LORD and waited for an answer, and the answer told him both to go and what would happen. Then, having recovered all, he refused to let two hundred exhausted men be cut out of the spoil by the sons of Belial among his own troops, and made it a statute in Israel that the man who keeps the baggage shares with the man in the line. Recovery, and then justice in the division of it, on the same day.

pos: n. pl. (the border cities or marches of a country)
etymology: From Old French frontier, the front or border, from Latin frons, the forehead. The Authorized Version uses the plural once, in the oracle against Moab, of the border cities God would open.
biblical_def: Therefore, behold, I will open the side of Moab from the cities, from his cities which are on his frontiers, the glory of the country, Bethjeshimoth, Baalmeon, and Kiriathaim. Moab's border fortresses are called the glory of the country, and they are named one by one before they are opened. The charge against Moab in the previous verse is not military but verbal: because that Moab and Seir do say, Behold, the house of Judah is like unto all the heathen. They had watched their kinsmen fall and drawn the conclusion that Judah's God was nothing special. Ezekiel 25 works through four such neighbours — Ammon, Moab, Edom, and the Philistines — and the offence in every case is what they said and felt while Jerusalem burned: Aha, against my sanctuary; thou hast clapped thine hands, and stamped with the feet, and rejoiced in heart with all thy despite. Obadiah brings the same charge against Edom in the sharpest form: thou shouldest not have looked on the day of thy brother in the day that he became a stranger. And the refrain that closes each oracle states the purpose of the whole chapter: they shall know that I am the LORD.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the marches; the border, confine or extreme part of a country, bordering on another country; in Scripture, the border cities of Moab, called the glory of the country.
webster_full: FRONTIER, n. The marches; the border, confine, or extreme part of a country, bordering on another country.
MARCHES, n. Borders; limits; confines; the frontiers of a country.
DESPITE, n. Extreme malice; violent hatred; malignity; malice irritated or enraged.
BORDER, n. The outer edge of anything; the extremity or exterior limit of a country or region.
VENGEANCE, n. The infliction of pain on another, in return for an injury or offense.
scriptures: Eze 25:9
Therefore, behold, I will open the side of Moab from the cities, from his cities which are on his frontiers, the glory of the country, Bethjeshimoth, Baalmeon, and Kiriathaim,
Eze 25:8
Thus saith the Lord GOD; Because that Moab and Seir do say, Behold, the house of Judah is like unto all the heathen;
And I will execute great vengeance upon them with furious rebukes; and they shall know that I am the LORD, when I shall lay my vengeance upon them.
Oba 1:12

But thou shouldest not have looked on the day of thy brother in the day that he became a stranger; neither shouldest thou have rejoiced over the children of Judah in the day of their destruction; neither shouldest thou have spoken proudly in the day of distress.
corruption_summary: Malice is assumed harmless while it stays at the level of speech and feeling; Ezekiel's oracles against four nations rest entirely on what those nations said and how they rejoiced at a neighbour's fall.
corruption_paragraphs: Nothing in Ezekiel 25 charges Moab, Ammon, Edom, or Philistia with invading Judah. The indictment is a saying, a clapping of hands, a stamping of the feet, and a rejoicing in heart with all thy despite. Secret satisfaction at a rival's ruin is treated as a real offence with real consequences, and the border fortresses called the glory of the country are opened because of it. Proverbs gives the private version of the same warning: rejoice not when thine enemy falleth, and let not thine heart be glad when he stumbleth, lest the LORD see it, and it displease him.

The aggravating factor in Obadiah is kinship. Edom was Esau, brother to Jacob, and the charge is a family charge — thou shouldest not have looked on the day of thy brother, neither shouldest thou have rejoiced over the children of Judah in the day of their destruction. The nearer the relation, the worse the gloating. That has an obvious application within the church, where a man's fall is sometimes received with a satisfaction nobody would say aloud, and where the refrain of the chapter still applies to the watchers as much as to the fallen: they shall know that I am the LORD.

pos: n. pl. (cases enclosing a light; carried by the band that arrested Christ)
etymology: From Latin lanterna, itself from Greek lampter, a torch. The Authorized Version uses the plural once, of the band of men and officers who came to Gethsemane with lanterns and torches and weapons.
biblical_def: Judas then, having received a band of men and officers from the chief priests and Pharisees, cometh thither with lanterns and torches and weapons. John names the equipment because the equipment is absurd. They came at night, armed, with lights, to take a man who had taught daily in the temple and who was standing in a garden waiting for them. And the arrest does not proceed as an arrest. Jesus therefore, knowing all things that should come upon him, went forth, and said unto them, Whom seek ye? — he asks the question, he identifies himself, he controls the scene. As soon then as he had said unto them, I am he, they went backward, and fell to the ground. An armed cohort with lanterns is put on its back by two words from an unarmed man, and then permitted to rise and do what it came for. He asks a second time, and adds a condition: if therefore ye seek me, let these go their way. John notes this fulfilled his own saying, Of them which thou gavest me have I lost none. The lanterns are the last irony — men carrying lamps to find the light of the world, who had told them plainly, I am the light of the world.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a case, usually of glass or horn, inclosing a light and protecting it from wind and rain; in Scripture, carried by the band that arrested Christ.
webster_full: LANTERN, n. A case, usually of glass or horn, inclosing a light, and preserving it from the wind and rain.
TORCH, n. A light to be carried in the hand, formed of some combustible substance.
BAND, n. A company of persons united in any common design; a body of armed men.
BETRAY, v.t. To deliver into the hands of an enemy by treachery or fraud, in violation of trust.
VOLUNTARY, a. Acting by choice, or without compulsion; proceeding from choice or free will.
scriptures: Joh 18:3
Judas then, having received a band of men and officers from the chief priests and Pharisees, cometh thither with lanterns and torches and weapons.
Joh 18:4
Jesus therefore, knowing all things that should come upon him, went forth, and said unto them, Whom seek ye?
Joh 18:6
As soon then as he had said unto them, I am he, they went backward, and fell to the ground.
Joh 8:12
Then spake Jesus again unto them, saying, I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life.
corruption_summary: The passion is read as a tragedy that overtook Jesus, a good man destroyed by powers greater than himself; John presents an arrest in which the arrested party asks the questions, puts the cohort on the ground, and sets the terms.
corruption_paragraphs: John 18 is written to make one point about the cross before the cross arrives: nobody took Christ's life from him. He had said it plainly — therefore doth my Father love me, because I lay down my life, that I might take it again. No man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again. The garden scene is that sentence acted out. Knowing all things that should come upon him, he goes forward to meet the lanterns rather than away from them, and the cohort that fell to the ground got up only because he let the arrest proceed.

The other half of the passage is the shepherd's clause, and it is easily missed among the drama. If therefore ye seek me, let these go their way. He negotiates the release of eleven frightened men while being taken himself, and John tells us why it is recorded: that the saying might be fulfilled which he spake, Of them which thou gavest me have I lost none. The definite, effectual keeping of those the Father gave the Son is not a later doctrinal construction. It is stated in a garden, under lantern light, at the worst moment of the disciples' lives.

pos: n. (the timber of the ark; a wood not otherwise identified in Scripture)
etymology: A transliteration of the Hebrew gopher, which occurs only here; the ancients connected it with resinous or pitch-bearing trees, and the same verse mentions pitching the ark within and without with pitch. The Authorized Version does not translate it, which is an honest confession that the tree is unknown.
biblical_def: Make thee an ark of gopher wood; rooms shalt thou make in the ark, and shalt pitch it within and without with pitch. The instruction is one line in a set of the most specific building instructions in Scripture: the length three hundred cubits, the breadth fifty, the height thirty, a window, a door in the side, with lower, second, and third stories. God gave the dimensions and the timber and the sealing compound, and Noah's obedience is recorded in a sentence the chapter repeats: Thus did Noah; according to all that God commanded him, so did he. Hebrews supplies the inward account of that outward obedience: by faith Noah, being warned of God of things not seen as yet, moved with fear, prepared an ark to the saving of his house; by the which he condemned the world, and became heir of the righteousness which is by faith. Things not seen as yet — there had been no flood, and by many accounts no rain as men knew it. He built for a century on a word. And when the animals and the family were aboard, the last detail of the boarding belongs to God alone: and the LORD shut him in.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a kind of wood of which Noah's ark was made, supposed by some to be cypress or a resinous tree; the word is not elsewhere used.
webster_full: GOPHER, n. A kind of wood of which Noah's ark was made; supposed to be a resinous tree, as the cypress or pine.
ARK, n. A small close vessel, chest or coffer; the vessel in which Noah and his family were preserved during the deluge.
PITCH, n. A thick tenacious substance, the juice of a species of pine or fir; used to caulk vessels.
DELUGE, n. A general flood of water; an inundation; particularly, the great flood in the days of Noah.
FAITH, n. The assent of the mind to the truth of what God has revealed; a firm and cordial belief.
scriptures: Gen 6:14
Make thee an ark of gopher wood; rooms shalt thou make in the ark, and shalt pitch it within and without with pitch.
Gen 6:22
Thus did Noah; according to all that God commanded him, so did he.
Gen 7:16
And they that went in, went in male and female of all flesh, as God had commanded him: and the LORD shut him in.
Heb 11:7

By faith Noah, being warned of God of things not seen as yet, moved with fear, prepared an ark to the saving of his house; by the which he condemned the world, and became heir of the righteousness which is by faith.
corruption_summary: The flood is reclassified as regional myth or as a borrowed legend, which severs it from the New Testament's use of it as a historical judgment and a pattern of the judgment to come.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary holds a historical Noah and a historical worldwide flood, and it does so because the New Testament does. Christ compared his own coming to it: as the days of Noe were, so shall also the coming of the Son of man be, for as in the days that were before the flood they were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the day that Noe entered into the ark, and knew not until the flood came, and took them all away. Peter argues from it twice, once for the certainty of judgment on the ungodly and once against the scoffers who say all things continue as they were from the beginning, and his answer is that they are willingly ignorant of a world that being overflowed with water, perished.

What the text does not do is pretend to more precision than it has. Nobody knows what gopher wood was, and the Authorized Version leaves the Hebrew word standing rather than guessing, which is a small model of translation honesty. The dimensions, the pitch, the door in the side, the years of building in front of a mocking world, and the LORD shutting the door himself are all given. The species of tree is not, and the salvation of the house never depended on the reader knowing it.
